ABSTRACT
The thermal management of ultra-high heat flux chips has become an urgent problem that needs to be addressed.
For the manifold microchannels, previous studies have generally treated the hot manifold side and cold manifold 
side as a whole, considering that when the structure of one side changes, the other side should maintain the same 
symmetrical structural configuration.
This paper 
focuses on this novel design concept and proposes a new manifold microchannel (termed PFMMC).
First, the hot manifold side 
have the same spanwise width, rather than the gradually expanding structure corresponding to the cold manifold 
side.
Second, microfins are added only to the hot-side microchannels.
Third, the microchannels have a narrow 
inlet and wider outlet to complement the fins.

Tuckerman and Pease [ 10 , 11 ] were the first to apply microchannel for 
cooling electronic chips (microchannel heat sink, MCHS), achieving a 
high heat flux of 790 W/cm
2 
with a Δ P of 214 kPa.
The maximum 
temperature rise of the heated surface was 71
◦
C higher than that of the 
inlet cooling water, demonstrating the significant advantage of micro -
channel over conventional-scale channel.
To address this, Harpole and 
Eninger [ 12 ] proposed the manifold microchannel heat sink (HEMMC, 
hereafter), which not only improves heat transfer capability signifi -
cantly but also reduces the flow distance markedly.
Subsequently, van 
Erp et al.[ 13 ] identified the significant flow imbalance in the HEMMC 
and modified the manifold flow cross-sectional area: it decreases for the 
cold fluid and increases for the hot fluid along the flow direction, 
effectively reducing flow imbalance between microchannels (EMMC, 
here after).
Since the publication of Refs [ 12 , 13 ], many researches have been 
conducted from various aspects, including channel structure [ 14 – 19 ], 
flow distribution [ 20 – 23 ], and adding fins [ 24 – 26 ], achieving signifi -
cant progress [ 27 – 29 ].
If flow disturbing structures are added to the lower 
microchannels on the cold manifold side, the same flow disturbing 
structures are added to the lower microchannels on the hot manifold 
side.
Therefore, to 
enhance the heat transfer of the manifold microchannels, the first step 
should be to enhance heat transfer at the hot manifold side and find 
ways to reduce its thermal resistance.
This includes three main aspects:
First, the hot manifold shape and cross-sectional width no longer 
adopt a symmetric configuration with the cold manifold side but are 
changed independently to investigate the effects of different hot 
manifold side cross-sectional shapes and widths on overall performance.
Second, fins are added only to the hot manifold side while main -
taining smooth channels on the cold manifold side, and the effects of fin 
diameter and number on flow and heat transfer performance are 
investigated.
Third, the microchannel widths on both the cold manifold side and 
hot manifold side are adjusted separately to match the fins added to the 
hot manifold side.
This ensures that when fins are added, they can fully 
exert their enhancement capability without excessively blocking the

The hot manifold shape and width are significant factors for heat 
transfer and Δ P .
To thoroughly investigate the ef -
fects of hot manifold shape and width on MMC heat transfer perfor -
mance, this paper systematically compares, for the first time in the 
literatures, the comprehensive performance of five structures: expand -
ing (Case 1), tapering (Case 2), uniform cross-section (Case 3), reduced 
width (Case 4), and magnified width (Case 5), and the results are shown 
in Figs.
Except the hot manifold shape and width, all 
other geometric parameters remain identical among these different 
structures.
No fins are added in any of the five cases.
The results of Cases 3 - 5 reveal the effects of the width of the 
manifold hot side.

8 (a), it can be observed that compared with Case 1, 
Case 2 has a larger proportion of coolant mass flow in the front micro -
channels relative to the total flow.
This is because Case 2 has a wider 
front hot manifold than Case 1, which shortens the front microchannel 
path, allowing more coolant to flow from the cold channel side to the hot 
channel side through the front microchannels.
How -
ever, the mass flow rate in the middle microchannels of Case 2 actually 
decreases, which explains why the hot spot region shifts to the right as 
shown in Fig.
Furthermore, since Case 3 shortens the flow path of most micro -
channels, it achieves a smaller pressure drop compared with Cases 1,2.
8 (b), the flow distribution among 
different microchannels in Case 3 is notably more uniform, with σ
u 
reduced by 75.06 % and 80.94 % compared with Case 1 and Case 2, 
respectively.

Furthermore, as W
h 
increases, the mass flow rates 
among different microchannels tend to become more consistent, leading 
to a 79.90 % reduction in σ
u 
for Case 5 compared with Case 4.
Fifth, compared with Case 5, Case 4 incorporates a narrower hot 
manifold width.
This geometric modification enlarges the microchannel 
region situated directly beneath the manifold ’ s solid section.
Since the 
fluid cross-sectional area within this microchannel zone is smaller than 
that of the hot manifold side, flow velocity is correspondingly enhanced, 
thereby improving convective heat transfer performance.
Therefore, when designing manifold microchannel structures, a 
uniform cross-sectional structure should be adopted for the hot channel, 
and W
h 
should be increased within a reasonable range to achieve 
optimal overall performance.
Effects of pin fin diameter (d) and number (N)
As indicated above, the microchannels on the cold manifold side 
possess high heat transfer capability due to the lower fluid temperature 
and the impinging flow pattern for heat transfer between the fluid and 
the heated surface.
Therefore, adding additional pin fins in the cold-side 
microchannels would yield relatively small heat transfer enhancement 
benefits.
At the hot manifold side, the heat transfer in microchannels is a 
conventional convective process, which results in significantly reduced 
heat transfer capability compared with the cold side, thus leading to 
notably higher heated surface temperatures beneath the hot manifold 
than beneath the cold manifold.
To enhance the overall performance of 
the EMMC, the primary focus should be on strengthening heat transfer 
within the hot channels.
Therefore, in this study, pin fins are only added 
at the hot manifold side ( Fig.

14 , it can be observed that, compared with the EMMC 
without pin fins (Case 5), the minimum reductions in T
w,max 
and T
h,ave 
for Cases 6-8 exceeded 1.74 K and 1.52 K, respectively, resulting in h and 
Nu values increased by at least more than 13.43 %.
This indicates that 
the addition of pin fins in the hot channels plays a significant role in 
controlling the heated surface hot spot temperature and improving the 
Fig.

The major change occurs 
by adding pin fin because the flow in the hot manifold changes from 
smooth channel flow into a bundle crossflow.
This not only effectively 
increases the heat transfer surface area within the thermal channel, but 
the presence of the tube bundle also disrupts the boundary layers 
development in the microchannels, thereby significantly enhancing 
convective heat transfer.
This is because pin 
fins are only added to the microchannels on the thermal manifold side, 
and only one row is installed in each microchannel.
15 and 16 , after adding pin fins, the flow velocity at the Y = 100 
µ m cross-section does not increase significantly.
This indicates that adding pin fins only 
to the microchannels on the thermal manifold side can significantly 
enhance heat transfer capability while maintaining the pressure drop 
increase within an acceptable range.
Apart from further increase 
heat transfer area larger diameter increases the blockage ratio of the 
channel, resulting in increased local fluid velocity.
Additionally, larger 
pin fins generate larger-scale vortex which enhances fluid mixing 
effects.

However, the increase in pin fins quantity also results in

Therefore, finding the balance between heat transfer and pres -
sure drop is a factor that needs to be considered in practical engineering 
applications.

effect of the coolant on the heat transfer surface, thus leading to higher

However, the reduction in W

also results in a 
smaller cross-sectional area for the coolant entering the lower micro -

19 (a) in -

However, this results in excessive coolant mass flow distribution in the 
front microchannels, while the mass flow rate in the rear microchannels 
becomes lower than the average value.
This leads to the appearance of 
high-temperature regions in the rear microchannels for Case 9, as shown

Based on the above studies, a nearly optimized structure (Case 13) is 
obtained (See Table 2 ), which has a minimum length of 1.2 mm.

is significantly higher than that under the rear microchannels, with a 
very obvious temperature gradient along the flow direction.

Performance impact mechanisms of inter-layer alignment deviation
In heat exchanger manufacturing, when structures are designed with 
geometric symmetry, the integration of the microchannel layer and 
Fig.

However, the asymmetric 
design proposed in this study faces more significant challenges during 
practical manufacturing — namely, ensuring precise alignment between 
the microchannel layer and the manifold layer.
Specifically, the hot side 
of the manifold layer must precisely align with the pin-fin distribution 
region, while the cold side must correspond accurately to the region 
without pin-fins.
27 , Case 16 represents a configuration 
where pin-fins are positioned at the center of the repeating unit, while 
Case 17 represents a layout where pin-fins are distributed on the cold 
manifold side of the repeating unit.
Comparing these two configurations 
with the original design (Case 13, where pin-fins are located on the hot 
manifold side) provides deep insights into the influence of inter-layer 
Fig.

Comparative analysis of Case 13 and Case 16 reveals that when pin 
fins are relocated from the hot manifold side to the center position of the 
repeating unit, both T
w,max 
and T
h,ave 
improve significantly, decreasing 
by 1.50 K and 2.92 K, respectively.
Further comparison between Case 13 and Case 17 reveals that when 
the pin fin position is completely relocated from the hot manifold side to 
the cold manifold side, T
w,max 
actually deteriorates, increasing by 2.77 K, 
while T
h,ave 
improves, decreasing by 1.64 K.
28 pre -
sents the temperature distribution contours of the heated surface for 
Cases 16 and 17, providing an intuitive visualization of how variations 
in pin fin positioning affect the temperature field.
Comprehensive analysis indicates that as the pin fin position shifts 
from the hot manifold side toward the cold manifold side, despite po -
tential improvements in localized heat transfer performance, the overall 
performance exhibits a gradual deterioration trend.
This finding carries 
significant implications for engineering practice: during actual 
manufacturing processes, if technological conditions permit, efforts 
should be made to ensure precise alignment of pin fins with the hot 
manifold side of the manifold layer to achieve optimal comprehensive 
performance.
This conclusion further validates the rationality of the 
asymmetric design principle proposed in this research and its potential 
in enhancing the performance of microchannel heat exchangers.
Micro-feature fabrication process
The core feature of the PFMMC is the integration of high-aspect-ratio 
microchannels and micro-pin-fin arrays on a silicon substrate.
It is therefore ideally suited for fabricating the microchannels and pin- 
fins designed in this study.

For the com -
plex layout in this paper, which includes both microchannels and micro- 
pin-fins, this could result in non-uniform etch depths.
This allows for real-time monitoring of the etching process 
to precisely control the final depth, thereby ensuring structural fidelity.
Multi-layer chip alignment and bonding
The realization of the PFMMC requires the precise alignment and 
hermetic bonding of the silicon wafer with fabricated microchannels 
(the channel layer) to another layer containing the manifold structure 
(the manifold layer).
Inter-layer alignment: The asymmetric design proposed herein, 
where the hot and cold sides of the manifold correspond to regions with 
and without pin-fins below, respectively, places stringent demands on 
inter-layer alignment accuracy.
Anodic 
bonding creates a high-strength, hermetic seal, ensuring leak-free 
operation of the coolant within the microchannels.
The main 
findings of this work are as follows: 
(1) The commonly used expanding hot manifold structure in the 
EMMC is not the most rational configuration.

(2) The addition of fins at the hot side of the microchannel can 
significantly enhance cooling performance, accompanied by a 
mild increase in Δ P .
(3) Both HEMMC and EMMC adopt uniform microchannel width.
However, this study shows that reducing W
c,in 
can greatly in -
crease the coolant flow rate in the front part of the micro -
channels, hence alleviate the temperature hotspot issue caused by 
insufficient coolant flow in the front microchannels.

The same logic becomes more explicit in RF and MMIC systems, where multiple closely spaced heat sources create both self-heating and lateral coupling. Experimentally, this architecture improved device response and weakened lateral thermal coupling when device spacing exceeded 600 μm at 100 mL/min[20]. range of 50–700, yielding a thermal performance evaluation criterion as 
high as 3.58 [13]. Follow-up studies further verified that such twisted 
leaf fins strengthen thermal exchange between the core flow and near- 
wall region while suppressing flow separation downstream, thus 
contributing to reduced pressure loss [14]. Tang et al. [15] incorporated 
airfoil fins into a jet-impingement microchannel heat sink (AF-JIMHS) 
and achieved improved temperature uniformity and reduced entropy 
generation by optimizing the inner fillet radius and chord length. 
Beyond microchannel heat sinks, airfoil-based concepts have also been 
explored in compact heat exchanger channels, such as printed circuit 
heat exchangers (PCHEs), and systematically optimized to balance heat 
transfer augmentation and flow resistance reduction [16,17]. Experi­
mental work by Shao et al. [18] demonstrated that high-turning-angle 
airfoil microfins with continuously varying pitch can simultaneously 
enhance heat transfer and reduce pressure drop at low Reynolds 
numbers. As a well-established airfoil series standardized by the Na­
tional Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, NACA profiles allow precise 
and systematic geometric control through concise parametric defini­
tions. Wu et al. [19] numerically investigated NACA airfoil pin fins in an 
open microchannel heat sink and identified the asymmetric NACA6412 
profile as the optimal configuration in terms of overall thermohydraulic 
performance. Further parametric analyses revealed that NACA airfoil 
thickness, camber, and vertical spacing exert significant influences on 
the coupled flow and heat transfer behavior [20]. Airfoil-based config­
urations have also exhibited competitive thermohydraulic performance 
when applied to extreme working fluids, including supercritical CO2, 
molten salts, and liquid metals [21–26]. Nevertheless, the majority of 
existing studies focus on the isolated optimization of individual airfoil 
geometries or a limited number of geometric parameters. The effects of 
gradient airfoil combinations and cooperative array arrangements on 
global flow field regulation, near-wall flow organization, and thermo­
hydraulic performance over a wide operational range remain inade­
quately understood.

Biomimetic design strategies have been increasingly adopted in 
MCHS development to achieve simultaneous drag reduction and heat 
transfer enhancement by mimicking high-efficiency structures and 
mechanisms observed in nature [27]. For instance, Gao et al. [28] pro­
posed fish-shaped ribbed microchannels inspired by collective biological 
patterns; numerical results demonstrated enhanced heat transfer co­
efficients with acceptable pressure drop penalties. Li et al. [29] devel­
oped biomimetic vascular network structures for battery liquid cooling 
plates and realized reliable temperature control under various discharge 
rates. A recent comprehensive review emphasized the critical role of 
biomimetic and topological microchannel designs in heat transfer 
enhancement, particularly in improving temperature uniformity for 
microchannel heat sinks [30]. Within this framework, shark-skin- 
inspired surfaces, distinguished by ordered dermal denticles and 
riblet-like microtextures, have shown considerable potential for pro­
moting flow mixing and thinning the thermal boundary layer. Wang 
et al. [31] integrated denticle-inspired structures on the bottom wall of a 
biomimetic microchannel heat sink and revealed that their streamwise 
distribution and inclination angle significantly affect overall thermal 
performance. Shen et al. [32] proposed several configurations of shark- 
inspired rectangular ribbed microchannels to enhance heat transfer with 
low pressure drop and reduced thermodynamic irreversibility; staggered 
unequal-length ribs were found to deliver the best overall performance 
under specific geometric conditions. More recent passive microchannel 
designs include biomimetic trefoil ribs and cavities [33,34], ogive- 
shaped ribs and rib-cavity combinations [35,36], and NACA 2412 hy­
drofoil ribs arranged in different wall configurations [37]. These studies 
further show that the rib or cavity profile and its wall placement can 
regulate thermal-boundary-layer interruption and hydraulic loss. 
Although these studies demonstrate the effectiveness of structural bionic 
optimization, many designs remain limited to the simplified replication 
or isolated application of individual features. The fundamental mecha­
nisms linking systematic surface arrangements (e.g., denticle arrays) to

flow separation control, drag reduction, and coupled flow-heat transfer 
performance are still not fully elucidated. Bridging this knowledge gap is 
critical for the development of high-performance biomimetic micro­
channels that can consistently achieve superior heat transfer with low 
hydraulic losses.

Motivated by the riblet-like, non-smooth architecture of shark-skin 
dermal denticles and the favorable aerodynamic characteristics of 
NACA airfoils, the present study introduces a novel Shark-Scale Inspired 
NACA Gradient Airfoil Microtexture (SI-NGM) microtextured channel 
for high-performance microchannel heat sinks. Three-dimensional 
conjugate heat-transfer simulations are performed to systematically 
investigate the influences of denticle-inspired gradient airfoil rib ge­
ometry and arrangement on pressure drop and heat transfer character­
istics. The performance of SI-NGM IV S is also examined up to Re = 5000 
to determine whether its thermohydraulic advantage persists beyond 
the laminar range. Experiments on representative enlarged 3D-printed 
SI-NGM channels are then used to verify whether the flow and heat 
transfer characteristics of the biomimetic microchannels can also be 
observed beyond the idealized numerical model. A neighboring wall 
interaction framework is used to interpret the influence of the relative 
wall arrangement on the SSC dependent thermohydraulic response, 
while the optimal SI-NGM configuration is identified directly from f/f0, 
Nu/Nu0, and TPER. Finally, the energy-saving potential of the proposed 
designs is quantitatively evaluated using Fan's performance evaluation 
plot. By offering coordinated control of airfoil camber, chord length, 
array arrangement, and opposing-wall offset without additional active 
components, the proposed solution is relevant to compact cooling pas­
sages for electronics and other high-heat-flux energy systems where 
heat-removal capacity and pumping demand must be balanced.

Inspired by the riblet-like microstructures on shark-skin dermal 
denticles shown in Fig. 1(a) [38], we designed a denticle-inspired 
microtextured microchannel heat sink featuring Shark-Scale Inspired 
NACA Gradient Airfoil Microtextures (SI-NGM), as presented in Fig. 1
(d). The heat sink consists of uniformly distributed microchannels ar­
ranged periodically, as shown in Fig. 1(c). The present work examines 
the synergistic effects of the NACA airfoil profiles, denticle inspired units 
composed of five ribs, gradients in rib camber and chord length, and the 
planar or spatial arrangement of these units on heat transfer enhance­
ment, while quantifying the associated change in flow resistance. Fig. 1
(c) illustrates a representative heat sink comprising six parallel micro­
channels. Owing to the geometric symmetry of the microchannel array, 
symmetry boundary conditions were applied in ANSYS Fluent to reduce 
computational cost. The single microchannel shown in Fig. 1(b), with 
dimensions of 10 mm × 1.6 mm × 0.04 mm, was selected as the 
computational domain.

The chord lengths of the middle, secondary outer, and outermost

variations in airfoil camber influence the surrounding flow patterns and 
disturbance characteristics [39,40]. Consequently, the airfoil camber 
increases progressively from Type I to Type IV, while the chord length 
decreases from the middle to the outermost position, forming a gradient 
airfoil rib arrangement across the channel width.

The effects of different SI-NGM microchannel configurations on the 
flow and heat-transfer performance are shown in Fig. 8. At Re = 400, the 
near-wall velocity contours, streamlines, and velocity vectors fields 
exhibit regular patterns governed primarily governed by airfoil sym­
metry and rib arrangement. As shown in Fig. 8(a), the symmetric airfoil 
configuration (SI-NGM I) yields relatively uniform velocity contours, 
with a smooth transition from the leading edge stagnation region to the 
downstream acceleration region. By contrast, the asymmetric airfoil 
configuration (SI-NGM IV) produces noticeably distorted leading-edge

contours and an expanded high velocity zone because of the altered 
local pressure gradient. The staggered arrangement (S) improves the 
spatial connectivity of low velocity regions by optimizing the relative 
positions of adjacent ribs, whereas the parallel arrangement (P) tends to 
interrupt the flow because of the chord length differences within the rib 
array.

The streamline patterns in Fig. 8(b) further indicate that, for SI-NGM 
I, the streamlines remain largely parallel, suggesting weak interaction 
among different portions of the flow. For SI-NGM IV, the streamlines 
bend substantially and form more concentrated high velocity pathways. 
Under the staggered layout (S), the streamlines exhibit stronger 
deflection in multiple spatial directions, and the resulting mixing en­
hances transverse transport. This behavior is closely related to the 
pressure distribution induced by the airfoil geometry. An adverse pres­
sure gradient near the highly cambered leading edge promotes flow 
separation, while a subsequent favorable pressure gradient facilitates 
reattachment. As illustrated in Fig. 8(c), a stagnation region appears at 
the leading edge of each rib. A pronounced recirculation zone forms near 
the trailing edge of the outermost, highly cambered airfoil, whereas 
separation is weaker around the secondary outer ribs, and the central 
symmetric rib maintains a comparatively stable flow. These features 
reflect the combined effects of the gradients in airfoil camber and chord 
length and of the rib arrangement. When the airfoil set transitions from 
highly cambered asymmetric ribs near the sidewalls to a symmetric rib 
in the core, the flow evolves from strong near-wall disturbance toward a 
more stable core region. This reorganization promotes momentum and 
thermal-energy transport from the mainstream toward the wall, thereby 
intensifying heat transfer.

points in Region I (k < kP) indicate heat-transfer deterioration under the 
same pumping power, i.e., no energy-saving benefit. Region II (kP < k 
< kΔp) corresponds to heat-transfer enhancement under the same 
pumping power. Region III (kΔp < k < kV) represents heat-transfer 
enhancement under the same pressure drop, and Region IV (k > kV) 
represents heat-transfer enhancement under the same flow rate; Regions 
II – IV therefore indicate energy-saving potential under different con­
straints. In general, points closer to the Y-axis imply better hydraulic 
performance, whereas points closer to the X-axis imply weaker heat- 
transfer performance. A larger slope (k) indicates a more pronounced 
energy-saving effect.

The symbols P, Δp, and V denote equal pumping power, equal 
pressure drop, and equal flow rate, respectively. The slopes of the three 
demarcation lines were fitted from the numerical data, giving kP =
0.0584, kΔp = 0.1146, and kV = 1.

and LIGA with electroforming for metallic channel plates [1,11,30], 
whereas tool radius and burr formation make conventional micro mill­
ing less suitable for the thinnest ribs and airfoil trailing edges. These 
processes require greater tooling, inspection, and process control than 
straight ribs, but reusable masters and replication can reduce the unit 
cost of repeated production [1,30]. The added geometric complexity is 
therefore most defensible in compact heat sinks where high heat flux 
and limited pumping power make thermohydraulic performance a pri­
mary design consideration.

The effects of different SI-NGM microchannel configurations on the 
flow and heat-transfer performance are shown in Fig. 8. At Re = 400, the 
near-wall velocity contours, streamlines, and velocity vectors fields 
exhibit regular patterns governed primarily governed by airfoil sym­
metry and rib arrangement. As shown in Fig. 8(a), the symmetric airfoil 
configuration (SI-NGM I) yields relatively uniform velocity contours, 
with a smooth transition from the leading edge stagnation region to the 
downstream acceleration region. By contrast, the asymmetric airfoil 
configuration (SI-NGM IV) produces noticeably distorted leading-edge

contours and an expanded high velocity zone because of the altered 
local pressure gradient. The staggered arrangement (S) improves the 
spatial connectivity of low velocity regions by optimizing the relative 
positions of adjacent ribs, whereas the parallel arrangement (P) tends to 
interrupt the flow because of the chord length differences within the rib 
array.

The streamline patterns in Fig. 8(b) further indicate that, for SI-NGM 
I, the streamlines remain largely parallel, suggesting weak interaction 
among different portions of the flow. For SI-NGM IV, the streamlines 
bend substantially and form more concentrated high velocity pathways. 
Under the staggered layout (S), the streamlines exhibit stronger 
deflection in multiple spatial directions, and the resulting mixing en­
hances transverse transport. This behavior is closely related to the 
pressure distribution induced by the airfoil geometry. An adverse pres­
sure gradient near the highly cambered leading edge promotes flow 
separation, while a subsequent favorable pressure gradient facilitates 
reattachment. As illustrated in Fig. 8(c), a stagnation region appears at 
the leading edge of each rib. A pronounced recirculation zone forms near 
the trailing edge of the outermost, highly cambered airfoil, whereas 
separation is weaker around the secondary outer ribs, and the central 
symmetric rib maintains a comparatively stable flow. These features 
reflect the combined effects of the gradients in airfoil camber and chord 
length and of the rib arrangement. When the airfoil set transitions from 
highly cambered asymmetric ribs near the sidewalls to a symmetric rib 
in the core, the flow evolves from strong near-wall disturbance toward a 
more stable core region. This reorganization promotes momentum and 
thermal-energy transport from the mainstream toward the wall, thereby 
intensifying heat transfer.

Fig. 9 summarizes the normalized friction factor (f/f0), normalized 
Nusselt number (Nu/Nu0), and TPER for the different SI-NGM micro­
channels. Increasing the asymmetry of the outer ribs from Type I to Type 
IV strengthens flow disturbance and therefore increases f/f0. For

staggered arrangement (S) consistently yields lower f/f0 than the par­
allel arrangement (P), consistent with the improved flow continuity 
observed in Fig. 8. Enhanced mixing associated with separation from the 
highly cambered ribs produces a marked increase in Nu/Nu0 as airfoil 
asymmetry increases. At Re = 1200, Nu/Nu0 increases from 1.39 for SI- 
NGM I S and increases to 1.42 for the most asymmetric configuration, SI- 
NGM IV S. In addition, the Nu/Nu0 values for staggered channels exceed 
those of the corresponding parallel arrangements at all Re, indicating a 
consistent heat transfer advantage for the staggered arrangement.

Comprehensive TPER analysis indicates that the TPER values for all 
structures increase with increasing Re. Among them, SI-NGM IV S 
consistently delivers the best performance, with TPER rising from 1.065 
at Re = 200 to 1.317 at Re = 1200. This configuration combines a 
gradient asymmetric airfoil rib set with a staggered layout. The simul­
taneous increase in Nu/Nu0 and limited growth of f/f0 indicate that this 
arrangement provides a favorable balance between heat transfer 
enhancement and flow resistance.

Fig. 10 shows the cross sectional velocity distributions in the SI-NGM 
I S channel for different rib spacing ratios (t/s) and rib height ratios (h/ 
s). As shown in Fig. 10(a), when t/s = 0.2, the high velocity regions are 
mainly confined to the vicinity of each airfoil rib. Local high velocity 
bands form on both sides of the leading edge because of flow contrac­
tion, and the disturbances induced by individual ribs remain relatively 
isolated. When t/s increases to 0.4, corresponding to a smaller rib 
spacing at fixed rib thickness, the interaction between neighboring ribs 
becomes stronger. The accelerated flow regions between ribs gradually 
connect and form more continuous high velocity passages, enhancing 
momentum exchange and strengthens fluid interaction. When t/s rea­
ches 0.6, the rib array becomes excessively dense and the high velocity 
region extends farther in the streamwise direction. Consequently, the 
overall flow throughput decreases and the flow resistance increases 
markedly. These changes indicate that reducing rib spacing within an 
appropriate range can promote momentum exchange in both the 
streamwise and transverse directions and improve the overall flow 
distribution.

Fig. 10(b) illustrates how the rib height ratio (h/s) modifies the flow 
structures near the wall and between ribs. At h/s = 0.05, the flow field

from the wall toward the channel center and forming a clear velocity 
gradient. When h/s increases to 0.2, an evident high velocity region 
appears because of acceleration between adjacent ribs. Meanwhile, a 
high velocity jet develops in the gap between the rib tips of the outer­
most short chord ribs and the top wall. This jet connects the high ve­
locity regions on both sides of the ribs and enhances transverse flow 
connectivity. However, when h/s reaches 0.35, the clearance above the 
rib tips becomes too small, causing severe blockage. The high velocity 
region is then confined to the channel center. Although this can benefit 
heat transfer in the core region, it deteriorates the flow and heat transfer 
performance near the wall. These structural changes in flow structure 
directly affect both hydraulic resistance and heat transfer.

Fig. 11 presents the variations in f/f0, Nu/Nu0, and TPER with t/s, h/ 
s, and Re. For all Re considered, f/f0, Nu/Nu0, and TPER increase 
monotonically as t/s increases from 0.1 to 0.6. This indicates that, within 
the present operating range, the heat transfer enhancement associated 
with a higher rib density remains dominant over the accompanying 
increase in flow resistance. No inflection point in overall performance is

observed. At Re = 1200, the configuration with t/s = 0.6 achieves an 
approximately 32% higher TPER than that with t/s = 0.1.

In contrast, the effect of rib height is more complex. As h/s increases 
from 0.05 to 0.3, f/f0, Nu/Nu0, and TPER generally increase together, 
suggesting that a larger rib height effectively strengthens flow distur­
bance and heat transfer. When h/s increases further from 0.3 to 0.35, the 
effect becomes Re dependent. At low Re (Re = 200 to 400), Nu/Nu0 
increases only slightly while f/f0 rises sharply, leading to a reduction in 
TPER. At Re = 600, TPER remains nearly unchanged. At higher Re (Re =
800 to 1200), TPER increases again. These trends suggest that, at low Re, 
the flow is more susceptible to blockage, whereas at higher Re the in­
crease in Nu/Nu0 offsets more of the added resistance. When h/s = 0.4, a 
fully penetrating structure forms and the channel is completely 
segmented by the ribs, producing very large Nu/Nu0 and f/f0. The 
resulting TPER is outstanding over the full Re range. Accordingly, rib 
height should be selected according to the primary operating range. For 
low Re operation (Re < 600), a moderate height of 0.25 ≤h/s ≤0.3 is 
recommended to avoid blockage. For higher Re operation (Re ≥600), h/

conclusions.text:
The main parametric analysis was limited to Re = 200–1200 because 
the proposed microchannel is intended to enhance heat transfer at low 
pumping demand. To examine its applicability beyond the laminar 
range, Rec and SI-NGM IV S were further simulated at Re = 1600, 2000, 
2400, 2800, 3200, 4000, and 5000 under the same geometric and 
thermal boundary conditions. The cases at Re = 1600–3200 were used to 
examine the expected transition interval, whereas Re = 4000 and 5000 
were used to assess turbulent operation. The exact transition interval 
depends on the channel geometry and wall texture [48]. SI-NGM IV S 
was selected because it provided the best overall performance among 
the single-wall configurations.

As shown in Fig. 15, f/f0 increases from 1.254 at Re = 1200 to a 
maximum of 1.490 at Re = 2800, while Nu/Nu0 reaches its maximum of 
1.760 at Re = 2400. TPER rises from 1.317 at Re = 1200 to 1.555 at Re =
2400, then decreases to 1.240 and 1.164 at Re = 4000 and 5000, 
respectively. The best overall balance therefore occurs at Re = 2400, 
while TPER remains greater than unity throughout the investigated 
range, including at the two turbulent conditions examined.

The increase in TPER up to Re = 2400 indicates that the additional 
heat transfer produced by separation, reattachment, and transverse 
mixing around the ribs grows faster than the associated friction penalty 
as the flow approaches transition. Beyond the peak, turbulent transport 
in Rec becomes stronger, reducing the additional benefit of the mixing 
generated by SI-NGM, while the ribs continue to impose form drag. The 
relative Nu/Nu0 and TPER therefore decrease, consistent with the non­
monotonic PEC reported for protrusion enhanced rectangular micro­
channels [48]. This decrease represents a reduction in relative 
advantage rather than heat transfer deterioration, because both ratios 
remain above unity at Re = 5000. However, the higher velocities 
required at these Reynolds numbers also increase the absolute pumping 
demand. Consequently, the laminar and early transition regimes remain 
more relevant to the intended low pumping power operation, even 
though SI-NGM IV S retains a thermohydraulic advantage at the two 
turbulent conditions examined.

By integrating shark-skin denticle morphology with NACA airfoil 
geometry, a novel denticle-inspired gradient airfoil microtextured 
channel (SI-NGM) was proposed. Its flow dynamics and thermohy­
draulic performance in microscale heat exchangers were investigated 
numerically and experimentally, with the main conclusions as follows:

metric airfoils near the walls to a symmetric airfoil in the core, 
combined with a staggered arrangement, effectively balances 
flow disturbance and stability. The SI-NGM IV S configuration 
achieves the optimal thermohydraulic performance within the 
original Re = 200–1200 parametric range, with a TPER of 1.317 
at Re = 1200.
(2) The independent roles of two key geometric parameters, the rib 
thickness-to-spacing ratio (t/s) and the rib height-to-spacing ratio 
(h/s), were quantified. Reducing rib spacing strengthens inter-rib 
flow interactions, which increases resistance, but the heat- 
transfer gain remains dominant over the examined range. When 
t/s increases from 0.1 to 0.6, TPER at Re = 1200 increases by 
approximately 32%. The optimal rib height depends on operating 
conditions. For Re < 600, a moderate rib height of 0.25 ≤h/s ≤
0.3 is recommended to avoid flow blockage; for Re ≥600, h/s can 
be increased to about 0.35 to obtain a larger heat transfer gain 
despite the additional resistance. A fully penetrating structure 
with h/s = 0.4 exhibits the ultimate heat-transfer capability at the 
highest Reynolds numbers.

(3) The SSC strongly affects the balance between flow resistance and 
heat transfer under neighboring wall effects. At Re = 1200, SSC =
0.75 reduces f/f0 by 8.5% relative to SSC = 0 while maintaining 
nearly the same Nu/Nu0, increasing TPER from 1.332 to 1.374. 
The experimental comparison retains the numerical performance 
ordering for SSC = 0, −0.25, and 0.75, supporting the identifi­
cation of SSC = 0.75 as the best overall arrangement among the 
examined cases. The neighboring wall framework connects this 
favorable balance with the spatial coordination of disturbances 
generated by the opposing textures and provides a basis for 
optimizing double-wall arrangements.
(4) All biomimetic microchannels exhibit evident energy-saving po­

tential based on Fan performance evaluation plots. SI-NGM IV S 
shows the best energy-saving performance among the single-wall 
designs, while SSC = −0.25 is optimal on the Fan plot among the 
examined double-wall arrangements. The energy-saving benefit 
weakens when Re > 1000.
(5) At higher Reynolds numbers, SI-NGM IV S maintains a thermo­

hydraulic advantage relative to Rec. TPER reaches 1.555 at Re =
2400 and remains 1.240 and 1.164 at Re = 4000 and 5000, 
respectively. The maximum occurs within the range examined for 
transition, and the decline after the peak shows that the relative 
advantage is reduced before fully turbulent operation, although 
TPER remains above unity at the two turbulent conditions 
examined.

The present conclusions apply to the investigated geometric and 
Reynolds-number ranges and to the idealized target-scale surface con­
ditions used in the numerical model. The cross scale experiments vali­
date the dimensionless trends and performance ordering of 
representative configurations, while the effects of target-scale 
manufacturing tolerance and roughness require further quantification. 
Future work will therefore combine target-scale fabrication with sys­
tematic tolerance and roughness studies, direct pumping power mea­
surements, and quantitative analyses of velocity, vorticity, local Nu, and 
thermal boundary layer development to define the operating and 
manufacturing ranges in which SI-NGM provides a practical advantage 
over simpler ribbed channels.

Conventional cooling schemes present constant hA (where h is the
convective heat transfer coeﬃcient and A the heat exchange surface)
values along the coolant ﬂow path, resulting in temperature non-uni-
formities (Fig. 1a). For this kind of cooling solutions, the only way to
reduce the temperature non-uniformities is to increase the ﬂow rate.
But this involves huge increases in the pressure drop and, therefore, of
the pumping power. In order to avoid this drawback, the convection
thermal resistance must be reduced along the ﬂow path, compensating
for the increase in ﬂow temperature, which can also be considered as an
additional thermal resistance since the available (Tﬂuid(x)-Twall) reduces
compared to (Tﬂuid,in-Twall) as we progress along the microchannel
(Fig. 1b).
With the aim of improving the temperature uniformity while
maintaining the overall thermo-hydraulic performance, Rubio-Jimenez
et al. [32] [33], proposed a micro pin-ﬁn heat sink with variable ﬁn
density as an alternative for cooling the next generation of IC chips.
They demonstrated, for a pumping power of 0.04 W/cm2 and a heat
ﬂux of 230 W/cm2, an overall value of the temperature gradient of
1.63 °C/mm, which was four times lower than the temperature gradient
generated in rectangular microchannel heat sinks subject to similar
sizes and operating conditions.
Other studies [34–38] focused on hybrid Jet impingement/micro-
channel (JIMC) cooling devices and validated their capacity to coun-
teract the coolant temperature increase and, therefore, to provide a
nearly constant (or even decreasing) temperature distribution of the
cooled object along the ﬂow path. This eﬀect is obtained by tailoring, at
the design stage, the widths of the channel to the local need of heat
extraction capacity (Fig. 2). The slot jet-impingement used as the
inlet allows to reduce the coolant ﬂow path and to tailor, by adjusting
the slot width, the local heat extraction capacity at the center of the
cooling device [39].
The main goal of this paper is to introduce a new hybrid cooling
scheme that replaces the longitudinal ﬁns of the microchannels sections
by a matrix of pin-ﬁns, named hereafter JIPF_A1. This device takes

advantage of the Hybrid jet impingement/microchannels cooling de-
vice improvements with respect to conventional microchannels while
oﬀering the possibility to vary the heat exchange surface in two di-
rections. In a ﬁrst step, the new hybrid Jet Impingement/Pin Fin matrix
(JIPF) cooling scheme performance is assessed and compared numeri-
cally
and
experimentally
with

Microchannels for a comparable layout, in order to isolate the eﬀect of
the geometry of the heat exchange area from its distribution. Once
validated, the numerical model is used to assess the impact of the pin
ﬁns distribution on the thermo-hydraulic performance in order to
identify the key factors for design.

The JIPF cooling scheme entails two well-diﬀerentiated areas. The
ﬁrst corresponds to a cooling system using jet impingement while the
second consists of a series of pin-ﬁn rows. To achieve a uniform wall
temperature even though the ﬂuid temperature will increase along the
ﬂow path, the conﬁguration must be deﬁned to locally adapt the con-
vective thermal resistance.
To increase, along the ﬂow path, the convective heat transfer
coeﬃcient, h, and the heat exchange surface, A, the density of pin ﬁns is
increased. In addition, the JIPF conﬁguration proposed here leverages
the increased h due to the impinging jet. The heat sink design procedure
for variable hA with impinging jet is detailed by Riera et al. [38].
To allow comparison between the pin-ﬁn (JIPF) and microchannel
(JIMC) cooling schemes, the distribution of rows of pin-ﬁns in this work
(Fig. 3) is similar to rows of variable density microchannels in the
previous hybrid Jet Impingement/MicroChannels cooling scheme work

Fig. 16 presents a comparison of the contours of the velocity gen-
erated for both conﬁgurations along the ﬂow length for JIMC_A1 and
JIPF_A1 conﬁgurations when Rein = 1150 and heat power dissipated is
50 W/cm2. The impact that the pin-ﬁn conﬁguration generates on the
ﬂuid motion, and thus in the heat dissipation, is clearly observed in
these contours. The ﬂuid ﬂowing through the microchannel conﬁg-
uration has a straight motion. The interaction between the coolant and
the walls of the ﬁns is signiﬁcantly reduced, as the transverse compo-
nent of the coolant velocity (Vy) is reduced with respect to the JIPF
case. Furthermore, we can observe that the pin ﬁns generate a coolant
mixing along the entire coolant ﬂow path, with negative longitudinal
components of the velocity (Vx) after each pin ﬁn.

The modeling approach is also applied to evaluate alternate JIMC
and JIPF conﬁgurations. In particular, we have noticed that the initial
pin-ﬁn density can lead to a reduction of surface temperature along the
ﬂow (Fig. 7), suggesting that the reduction in thermal resistance due to
higher ﬁn density over-compensates for the ﬂuid temperature increase.
The basic cooling devices studied in previous sections are compared
against alternative cooling schemes, named JIMC_B1 and JIPF_B1
(Table 2), with lower densities of heat exchange elements (micro-
channels or pin ﬁns), aiming to prevent the overcooling and improve
uniformity. In addition, the high density of pin-ﬁns and microchannels
in the initial design can only lead to unnecessary pressure drop. These
new conﬁgurations with lower density are also proposed to achieve
similar thermal performance results while improving hydraulic per-
formance. The conﬁgurations presented in this section are evaluated for
Reynolds number ranging from 400 to 2200 (Fig. 17). The total thermal
power applied to the cooling layer is 250 W (q’’ = 50 W/cm2).

Figs. 14 and 17a demonstrate that the micro-pin-ﬁns oﬀers the
lowest maximum temperature for given heat power and ﬂow rate
conditions. Fig. 17b and c show that low-density conﬁgurations (both
for microchannels and pin-ﬁns) are optimum when temperature uni-
formity and low pumping power are required. The lower density con-
ﬁgurations (JIMC_B1 and JIPF_B1) show better temperature uniformity
and their thermal performance only depend slightly on ﬂow rate con-
ditions. The JIPF_A1 cooling scheme is recommended when the re-
duction of maximum chip temperature is the main goal, as shown in
Fig. 17a.
Further conﬁgurations are evaluated to analyze the eﬀect of pin-ﬁn
density in JIPF designs. The goal is to achieve lower values of maximum
temperature and temperature nonuniformity while minimizing the ratio
between pumping power consumed and heat power dissipated. Cooling
schemes (Table 3) and their variable pin-ﬁn densities along the ﬂow
path are shown in Fig. 18 a and b.

[42].

Overall, the highest density cooling scheme, JIPF_A1, shows the
lowest maximum chip temperature. The optimum temperature uni-
formity is obtained for JIPF_B2 scheme while JIPF_B3 scheme oﬀers the
best energetic performance. These results point to the need of speci-
fying, at the design stage, the performance required in terms of max-
imum temperature, pumping power and temperature uniformity in
order to choose adequately the most appropriate geometry.

A micro-pin-ﬁn heat sink with variable density is proposed with the
aim of improving the temperature uniformity of the cooled device. Its
thermo-hydraulic performance is assessed and compared to previous
cooling solutions. The experimental and numerical analysis presented
in this paper clearly states the beneﬁts of using increasing density of
pin-ﬁns along the ﬂow direction to reduce convection thermal re-
sistance to compensate for the ﬂow temperature increase, hence
keeping the surface temperature uniform. Furthermore, when com-
paring the pin-ﬁns to a similar approach based on rows of micro-
channels of varying density (JIMC), the micro-pin-ﬁn scheme (JIPF), in
its oﬀset pin-ﬁn conﬁguration, improves maximum temperature and

temperature uniformity at the Reynolds numbers and heat powers
proposed. The hydraulic performance, assessed through the ratio be-

obtained for the 4 ﬂow rates (Table 1) and the 2 cooling devices con-
sidered in this study, is represented in Fig. 7.
The uncertainty owing to the error of the TIM thickness measure-
ment of ± 5 μm can be valued with a margin of ± 1.1 °C. Added to the
uncertainty due to thermocouples measurement of ± 0.5 °C, the total
margin of error represented in the ﬁgure is ± 1.6 °C. Additionally, the
uncertainties in ﬂow rate measurements, pressure drop and electrical
power levels are ± 2%, ± 1% and ± 10 W respectively.
Experimentally, similar trends and values are obtained for both the
hybrid Jet Impingement/Microchannel (JIMC_A1) and the hybrid Jet
Impingement/Micro-pin-ﬁn (JIPF_A1) cooling devices. For the lowest
Reynolds number (Rein = 650), the temperature slightly increases along
the ﬂow path of the coolant, whereas for higher Reynolds numbers, the
temperature is quite uniform or even decreases. This trend is obtained
through the reduction of convective thermal resistance in the direction
of the ﬂow, which compensates the increase of the coolant temperature
in the same direction.
As a consequence, the performance of the device based on the ma-
trix of pin-ﬁns in terms of heat exchange is not very diﬀerent from the
one of the multi-row microchannel-based device. This fact is conﬁrmed
by the fact that the global thermal resistance coeﬃcients follow the
same trend for both cooling schemes (Fig. 8), reaching values of
Rt = 0.26 cm2 K/W for the highest Rein. The diﬀerence of global
thermal resistance coeﬃcients between the two cooling devices con-
sidered is below 7%. The thermal resistance is calculated by applying
the following equation:

The pressure drop caused by the cooling device is an important
parameter, since this value inﬂuences the parasitic power consumption

of the pump and, as a consequence, negatively aﬀects the energy bal-
ance of the system. Fig. 9 shows similar trends for both the JIMC_A1
and the JIPF_A1 cooling schemes. However, some diﬀerences are
measured for low and high Reynolds numbers. For Rein ≤1150, the
JIPF_A1 scheme generates lower pressure losses than the JIMC_A1 one.
While for Rein > 1500, the JIPF scheme oﬀers the largest values. This is
due to the fact that the pressure drop is caused by the wall friction and
separated ﬂow. It is presumed that for low Reynolds numbers, the re-
mains laminar and the highest heat exchange area of the microchannel
rows induces more pressure drop than in the case of the pin-ﬁns. When
the ﬂow rate increases (highest Reynolds numbers), separation is ex-
pected to occur behind the pin-ﬁns, generating increased losses com-
pared to the microchannel rows.

A conjugate numerical model has been developed and experimen-
tally validated in order to study the behavior of JIMC_A1 in previous
studies [36–38]. The same procedure is applied to JIPF_A1, in order to
carry out further studies on pin-ﬁn conﬁgurations. The geometric
complexity leads to a very high number of nodes and, thus, to very high
computational requirements and times, even by modeling a quarter of
the geometry by using the symmetries of the cooling scheme (x = 0 mm
and y = 0 mm). To further reduce the numerical load, a strip of the
device was considered instead, where symmetry boundary conditions
were deﬁned at the cutting planes shown in Fig. 10. It represents a
region in the center of the device, without considering side wall eﬀects.
The computational domain as shown in Fig. 10 has a width of 0.82 mm
and a length of 25 mm. The other boundary conditions are the imposed
mass ﬂow, the temperature at the inlet and the heat ﬂux on the bottom
wall, q’’ is set to 50 W/cm2. The energy equation is solved in the ﬂuid
and solid domains.

1) The system is in the steady state.
2) Water in single phase and laminar regime enters the system at 20 °C
under non-developed conditions.
3) The ﬂuid and solid thermal properties remain constant, except ﬂuid
viscosity, which is given by Equation (2) [40].

surement error is ± 1.6 °C (only represented for one point of the ﬁgure for easier interpretation).

524 800 tetrahedral elements distributed uniformly, except in the sec-
tion near the pin-ﬁn walls where a cell ratio of 1.025 is set. This mesh is
adapted to the pin-ﬁn shape. A mesh sensibility analysis was done in
order to arrive at the appropriate number of elements for achieving
satisfactory results.
The boundary conditions for the models are adjusted according to
the interaction of the ﬂuid with the surroundings. A constant mass ﬂow
rate is considered at the ﬂuid inlet section of the model. It is important
to highlight that the velocity proﬁle is not considered because of the
eﬀects of developing the boundary layer at this inlet section (which
otherwise becomes reduced), aﬀecting the goal of increasing the heat
transfer coeﬃcient. A constant heat ﬂux is imposed on the bottom wall
of the solid domain. Zero static pressure is assumed at the ﬂuid outlet
section. The walls between the domains are set as symmetry walls. The
upper wall of the channel and pin-ﬁns are set as adiabatic walls.

Energy balance was carried out for the system. The ﬂuid tempera-

The above-described modeling was validated against experimental
measurements shown in Fig. 5. Fig. 11 illustrates that the model is able
to successfully capture the JIPF_A1 cooling performance for the dif-
ferent ﬂow rates. The small discrepancy between the model and mea-
sured results can be attributed to minor deviations of actual ﬂow dis-
tribution in the heat sink from the modeled distribution due to TIM
inhomogeneities and potentially sidewall eﬀects neglected in the
model.
Once validated (Fig. 12), the numerical models are used to evaluate

To predict the performance of the cooling devices in several appli-

Fig. 14. For the range of power dissipated and ﬂow rates applied, the
pin-ﬁn scheme oﬀers lower maximum temperatures and better tem-
perature uniformity.

show that JIMC_A1 and JIPF_A1 conﬁgurations oﬀer similar results

shown in Table 1, the diﬀerence between the theoretical and experi-
mental values is lower than the uncertainty of the thermocouples
( ± 0.5 °C).

The temperature distribution along the ﬂow path of the coolant,
obtained for the 4 ﬂow rates (Table 1) and the 2 cooling devices con-
sidered in this study, is represented in Fig. 7.
The uncertainty owing to the error of the TIM thickness measure-
ment of ± 5 μm can be valued with a margin of ± 1.1 °C. Added to the
uncertainty due to thermocouples measurement of ± 0.5 °C, the total
margin of error represented in the ﬁgure is ± 1.6 °C. Additionally, the
uncertainties in ﬂow rate measurements, pressure drop and electrical
power levels are ± 2%, ± 1% and ± 10 W respectively.
Experimentally, similar trends and values are obtained for both the
hybrid Jet Impingement/Microchannel (JIMC_A1) and the hybrid Jet
Impingement/Micro-pin-ﬁn (JIPF_A1) cooling devices. For the lowest
Reynolds number (Rein = 650), the temperature slightly increases along
the ﬂow path of the coolant, whereas for higher Reynolds numbers, the
temperature is quite uniform or even decreases. This trend is obtained
through the reduction of convective thermal resistance in the direction
of the ﬂow, which compensates the increase of the coolant temperature
in the same direction.
As a consequence, the performance of the device based on the ma-
trix of pin-ﬁns in terms of heat exchange is not very diﬀerent from the
one of the multi-row microchannel-based device. This fact is conﬁrmed
by the fact that the global thermal resistance coeﬃcients follow the
same trend for both cooling schemes (Fig. 8), reaching values of
Rt = 0.26 cm2 K/W for the highest Rein. The diﬀerence of global
thermal resistance coeﬃcients between the two cooling devices con-
sidered is below 7%. The thermal resistance is calculated by applying
the following equation:

The pressure drop caused by the cooling device is an important
parameter, since this value inﬂuences the parasitic power consumption

of the pump and, as a consequence, negatively aﬀects the energy bal-
ance of the system. Fig. 9 shows similar trends for both the JIMC_A1
and the JIPF_A1 cooling schemes. However, some diﬀerences are
measured for low and high Reynolds numbers. For Rein ≤1150, the
JIPF_A1 scheme generates lower pressure losses than the JIMC_A1 one.
While for Rein > 1500, the JIPF scheme oﬀers the largest values. This is
due to the fact that the pressure drop is caused by the wall friction and
separated ﬂow. It is presumed that for low Reynolds numbers, the re-
mains laminar and the highest heat exchange area of the microchannel
rows induces more pressure drop than in the case of the pin-ﬁns. When
the ﬂow rate increases (highest Reynolds numbers), separation is ex-
pected to occur behind the pin-ﬁns, generating increased losses com-
pared to the microchannel rows.

A conjugate numerical model has been developed and experimen-
tally validated in order to study the behavior of JIMC_A1 in previous
studies [36–38]. The same procedure is applied to JIPF_A1, in order to
carry out further studies on pin-ﬁn conﬁgurations. The geometric
complexity leads to a very high number of nodes and, thus, to very high
computational requirements and times, even by modeling a quarter of
the geometry by using the symmetries of the cooling scheme (x = 0 mm
and y = 0 mm). To further reduce the numerical load, a strip of the
device was considered instead, where symmetry boundary conditions
were deﬁned at the cutting planes shown in Fig. 10. It represents a
region in the center of the device, without considering side wall eﬀects.
The computational domain as shown in Fig. 10 has a width of 0.82 mm
and a length of 25 mm. The other boundary conditions are the imposed
mass ﬂow, the temperature at the inlet and the heat ﬂux on the bottom
wall, q’’ is set to 50 W/cm2. The energy equation is solved in the ﬂuid
and solid domains.

1) The system is in the steady state.
2) Water in single phase and laminar regime enters the system at 20 °C
under non-developed conditions.
3) The ﬂuid and solid thermal properties remain constant, except ﬂuid
viscosity, which is given by Equation (2) [40].

Fig. 7. Temperature distribution measured by thermocouples at z = −1.25 mm at various Rein for JIMC_A1 and JIPF_A1 cooling schemes. The temperature mea-
surement error is ± 1.6 °C (only represented for one point of the ﬁgure for easier interpretation).

equations for both domains under the assumptions and boundary con-
ditions mentioned above.
Energy balance was carried out for the system. The ﬂuid tempera-
ture diﬀerence in the pin-ﬁn heat sink model was calculated from the
numerical results and compared with the analytical results. The average
temperature value at the ﬂuid inlet and outlet sections were determined
by numerical surface integration. The diﬀerence between numerical
and analytical outlet ﬂuid temperature with operating conditions of
200 ml/s of water and 50 W/cm2 of heat ﬂux is less than 0.7%.

The above-described modeling was validated against experimental
measurements shown in Fig. 5. Fig. 11 illustrates that the model is able
to successfully capture the JIPF_A1 cooling performance for the dif-
ferent ﬂow rates. The small discrepancy between the model and mea-
sured results can be attributed to minor deviations of actual ﬂow dis-
tribution in the heat sink from the modeled distribution due to TIM
inhomogeneities and potentially sidewall eﬀects neglected in the
model.
Once validated (Fig. 12), the numerical models are used to evaluate
diﬀerent local parameters at the chip level (z = 0 mm), which are not
available directly by measurements. Chip maximum temperature and
chip temperature nonuniformity (ΔT = Tmax-Tmin) are extracted from
the simulations and presented in Fig. 13. The main advantages of
JIPF_A1 versus JIMC_A1 scheme are the lower chip maximum tem-
perature and the higher chip temperature uniformity.
To predict the performance of the cooling devices in several appli-
cations, the modeling approach is applied to compare the cooling
schemes JIMC_A1 and JIPF_A1 at heat power dissipation ranging from
25 W/cm2 to 150 W/cm2 (corresponding to background and hotspot
zones, respectively, in microelectronics, or to heat ﬂuxes in dense array
CPV receivers) and Reynolds numbers from 400 to 2200. Maximum
temperature achieved at any point on the chip surface is plotted in
Fig. 14. For the range of power dissipated and ﬂow rates applied, the
pin-ﬁn scheme oﬀers lower maximum temperatures and better tem-
perature uniformity.
The pumping power is a good indicator for hydraulic performance
comparison. But the Figure of Merit deﬁned by the ratio between
pumping power consumed to heat power dissipated (Ppump/Pchip) is

preferred to compare the energetic performances [41] (Fig. 15). Results
show that JIMC_A1 and JIPF_A1 conﬁgurations oﬀer similar results
when Reynolds is small or heat power dissipated is above 50 W/cm2.

Fig. 11. Comparison of measured and modeled temperature distribution for the JIPF_A1 cooling device (z = −1.25 mm, q’’ = 50 W/cm2). The temperature mea-
surement error is ± 1.6 °C.

Fig. 12. Validation of the numerical model. The temperature measurement
error is ± 1.6 °C (only represented for one point of the ﬁgure for easier inter-
pretation).

Fig. 13. Maximum chip temperature (Tmax) and temperature nonuniformity
(ΔT) at z = 0 mm (just below the cooling device -see Fig. 5-) for JIMC_A1 and
JIPF_A1 cooling schemes (q’’ = 50 W/cm2).

Fig. 16. Velocity at the middle of the JIPF and JIMC section (z = 150 μm), Rein = 1150; q” = 50 W/cm2 (19.35 mm < x < 21.65 mm) (a) longitudinal component
Vx and (b) transverse component Vy.

Fig. 16 presents a comparison of the contours of the velocity gen-
erated for both conﬁgurations along the ﬂow length for JIMC_A1 and
JIPF_A1 conﬁgurations when Rein = 1150 and heat power dissipated is
50 W/cm2. The impact that the pin-ﬁn conﬁguration generates on the
ﬂuid motion, and thus in the heat dissipation, is clearly observed in
these contours. The ﬂuid ﬂowing through the microchannel conﬁg-
uration has a straight motion. The interaction between the coolant and
the walls of the ﬁns is signiﬁcantly reduced, as the transverse compo-
nent of the coolant velocity (Vy) is reduced with respect to the JIPF
case. Furthermore, we can observe that the pin ﬁns generate a coolant
mixing along the entire coolant ﬂow path, with negative longitudinal
components of the velocity (Vx) after each pin ﬁn.

The modeling approach is also applied to evaluate alternate JIMC
and JIPF conﬁgurations. In particular, we have noticed that the initial
pin-ﬁn density can lead to a reduction of surface temperature along the
ﬂow (Fig. 7), suggesting that the reduction in thermal resistance due to
higher ﬁn density over-compensates for the ﬂuid temperature increase.
The basic cooling devices studied in previous sections are compared
against alternative cooling schemes, named JIMC_B1 and JIPF_B1
(Table 2), with lower densities of heat exchange elements (micro-
channels or pin ﬁns), aiming to prevent the overcooling and improve
uniformity. In addition, the high density of pin-ﬁns and microchannels
in the initial design can only lead to unnecessary pressure drop. These
new conﬁgurations with lower density are also proposed to achieve
similar thermal performance results while improving hydraulic per-
formance. The conﬁgurations presented in this section are evaluated for
Reynolds number ranging from 400 to 2200 (Fig. 17). The total thermal
power applied to the cooling layer is 250 W (q’’ = 50 W/cm2).

Figs. 14 and 17a demonstrate that the micro-pin-ﬁns oﬀers the
lowest maximum temperature for given heat power and ﬂow rate
conditions. Fig. 17b and c show that low-density conﬁgurations (both
for microchannels and pin-ﬁns) are optimum when temperature uni-
formity and low pumping power are required. The lower density con-
ﬁgurations (JIMC_B1 and JIPF_B1) show better temperature uniformity
and their thermal performance only depend slightly on ﬂow rate con-
ditions. The JIPF_A1 cooling scheme is recommended when the re-
duction of maximum chip temperature is the main goal, as shown in
Fig. 17a.
Further conﬁgurations are evaluated to analyze the eﬀect of pin-ﬁn
density in JIPF designs. The goal is to achieve lower values of maximum
temperature and temperature nonuniformity while minimizing the ratio
between pumping power consumed and heat power dissipated. Cooling
schemes (Table 3) and their variable pin-ﬁn densities along the ﬂow
path are shown in Fig. 18 a and b.
The ﬁn area density (D) is deﬁned by the ratio between the circular
cross-sections of pin-ﬁns to the total rectangular area of the bottom wall
[42].

(c) Ppump/Pchip at z = 0 mm for conﬁgurations listed in Table 2 (q’’ = 50 W/
cm2).

The conﬁgurations presented in Table 3 are evaluated for Reynolds
numbers ranging from 400 to 2200. The total thermal power applied to
the cooling layer is 250 W (50 W/cm2).
Overall, the highest density cooling scheme, JIPF_A1, shows the
lowest maximum chip temperature. The optimum temperature uni-
formity is obtained for JIPF_B2 scheme while JIPF_B3 scheme oﬀers the
best energetic performance. These results point to the need of speci-
fying, at the design stage, the performance required in terms of max-
imum temperature, pumping power and temperature uniformity in
order to choose adequately the most appropriate geometry.

A micro-pin-ﬁn heat sink with variable density is proposed with the
aim of improving the temperature uniformity of the cooled device. Its
thermo-hydraulic performance is assessed and compared to previous
cooling solutions. The experimental and numerical analysis presented
in this paper clearly states the beneﬁts of using increasing density of
pin-ﬁns along the ﬂow direction to reduce convection thermal re-
sistance to compensate for the ﬂow temperature increase, hence
keeping the surface temperature uniform. Furthermore, when com-
paring the pin-ﬁns to a similar approach based on rows of micro-
channels of varying density (JIMC), the micro-pin-ﬁn scheme (JIPF), in
its oﬀset pin-ﬁn conﬁguration, improves maximum temperature and

temperature uniformity at the Reynolds numbers and heat powers

for the highest range of Reynolds number considered implies that they
can save more pumping power with respect to JIPF cooling schemes.
For a given Reynolds number, the performance of several pin ﬁns
distributions, assessed in identical conditions (Rein = 2200, q″ = 50 W/
cm2 and Tﬂuid,in = 20 °C), lead to a temperature uniformity of 2 °C, a
maximum chip temperature of 44,4 °C (for inlet ﬂow at 20 °C) and a
ratio between the pumping power and the chip power of 0.37%.
Nevertheless, the fact that each of these optimal results are obtained for
diﬀerent pin ﬁns distributions indicate that, at the design stage, the
performance goals for maximum temperature, uniformity and power
consumption must be precisely deﬁned and balanced.

ABSTRACT  
Maintaining temperature uniformity of the device is a crucial factor in reducing the risk of local overheating and 
ensuring high performance stability.
In this paper, we proposed a novel inner-fin microchannel (IFMC) cooling 
system based on the ideas of variable density microstructures and local densification design principles, and 
further established a parameterized model between the inner-fin height and heating condition for improving the 
temperature uniformity.
Moreover, the standard deviation of temperature (SDT) on the heating surface of the IFMC 
structure is much lower than that of the traditional microchannel (TMC) structure at the same inlet flow rate, 
with a decrease rate of over 96.05 %.
In 1981, Tuckerman and Pease [5] first proposed the concept of a 
parallel microchannel heat sink, which had high heat dissipation spe -
cific surface area and heat dissipation efficiency compared to traditional 
large channel.
Since then, many scholars have proposed various 
methods to improve microchannel cooling systems under high heat flux 
conditions.
These methods include studying interrupted and offset 
microchannel structure [6,7] , micro-pin – fin structure [8 – 10] , secondary 
flow [11,12] , pulse flow [13,14] , nanofluid [15,16] , surface modifica -
tion [17] , rough surface [18,19] , and more.

Finally, thermal physical

ABSTRACT  
Maintaining temperature uniformity of the device is a crucial factor in reducing the risk of local overheating and 
ensuring high performance stability.
In this paper, we proposed a novel inner-fin microchannel (IFMC) cooling 
system based on the ideas of variable density microstructures and local densification design principles, and 
further established a parameterized model between the inner-fin height and heating condition for improving the 
temperature uniformity.
The numerical simulation studies indicated the IFMC heat sink can maintain a high 
temperature uniformity under uniform and non-uniform heat flux densities.
Moreover, the standard deviation of temperature (SDT) on the heating surface of the IFMC 
structure is much lower than that of the traditional microchannel (TMC) structure at the same inlet flow rate, 
with a decrease rate of over 96.05 %.
These studies can provide reference for further design and development of 
equipment cooling systems with high temperature uniformity.

Compared to control the maximum temperature of electronic devices 
under high heat flux density, the issue of maintaining temperature 
uniformity is more important in certain situations [28,29] .
Firstly, 
temperature non-uniformity may cause local high temperatures, 
resulting in thermal deformation of electronic device structures.
Secondly, large temperature differences can cause local 
stress due to different expansion coefficients of different materials, 
which can result in severe fatigue failure [31] .
Therefore, maintaining tem -
perature uniformity is one of the most important conditions for ensuring 
the performance and reliability of miniaturized and integrated devices.
The main cause of temperature non-uniformity in devices can be 
attributed to two factors.
One is the fluid state change along the direc -
tion of flow, which leads to continuous decrease of the convective heat 
transfer coefficient along the flow direction in the device.
The variation 
of convective heat transfer coefficient will lead to temperature non- 
uniformity distribution on the heating surface.
The results 
showed that microchannel configurations with three and five channels 
arranged transversely can achieve the best temperature uniformity.
[34 – 36] confirmed that multi-scale leaf vein microchannels, spider 
web microchannels, and honeycomb structures have a more uniform 
flow distribution and better temperature uniformity than conventional 
microchannels.
It has been confirmed that these devices have higher tempera -
ture uniformity than conventional microchannels.
Compared to 
designing appropriate flow fields, variable-density microstructures can 
provide a more significant improvement in temperature uniformity.
Secondary flow, grooves, and micro-rib structures can be used to 
enhance fluid disturbance and improve the local convective heat 
transfer coefficient.
The study 
confirmed that the cooling setting could provide high temperature 
uniformity, with a temperature standard deviation of up to 0.8 
◦
C.
[45] proposed a novel enhancement called the variable density 
alternating obliquely truncated microchannel combined with oblique fin 
(AOTF-MC) to improve temperature uniformity.

[52] further utilized local microneedle fin clusters in

In summary, many scholars have conducted extensive research on 
temperature uniformity to ensure optimal performance of devices in 
typical operating conditions.
Firstly, 
in order to enhance the device ’ s reliability, it is necessary to further 
improve the temperature uniformity under high heat flux density.
Sec -
ondly, the two factors that cause device temperature non-uniformity 
often exist simultaneously in practice.
Thirdly, most of the current methods to improve 
temperature non-uniformity do not have a direct mathematical rela -
tionship with heat sink.
As a result, it is impossible to quantitatively 
design a cooling system that meets specific temperature non-uniformity 
requirements.
Based on the shortcomings of the above research, this 
paper proposes a new inner-fin microchannel (IFMC) structure that has 
higher heat dissipation capacity and maintains temperature uniformity 
compared to conventional microchannel structures.
This provides a reference 
for the further design and development of device cooling systems that 
require high temperature uniformity.

temperature uniformity in all directions of the structure.

Conclusion 
In this work, we proposed a novel inner-fin microchannel structure 
(IFMC) and derived a variable-area parameterized model based on 
temperature uniformity for the change of the inner-fin height along the 
flow direction.
Compared with the research work of previous scholars, 
the parameterized model established in this study directly associates 
temperature uniformity technical indicators with structural geometric 
parameters.
It has been verified through simulation that parameterized 
structures can achieve high-temperature uniformity of devices under 
uniform and non-uniform high heat flux heating conditions.

the TMC structure, and can achieve higher temperature uniformity on 
the heating surface.
The SDT value of the IFMC structure is much lower

sink by coupling genetic algorithm and CFD model
Ya Ge, Weixing Yin, Yousheng Lin, Kui He, Qing He

ABSTRACT
Wavy mini-channel heat sinks (MCHS) can disrupt the development of the thermal boundary layer, resulting in 
superior performance compared to straight MCHS.
For complete utilization of the coolant, this study proposed 
and optimized a non-uniform sinusoidal MCHS with varying wavelength or varying amplitude along the flow 
direction.
The optimization for five design variables was accomplished through a multi-objective genetic algo -
rithm, where the thermal resistance θ or the pressure drop Δ p were defined as two objectives.
Compared to the straight MCHS with different channel widths, the optimal designs achieved reductions 
of 27.74 % in θ or 59.51 % in Δ p .
Simultaneously, all the optimal values of the wavelength ratio and amplitude 
ratio indicate that enhancing the heat transfer performance downstream is more efficient.
Compared to the straight MCHS with the same Δ p , the best compromise solution with 
varying wavelength reduces the θ and the standard temperature deviation by 26.20 % and 76.98 % respectively, 
while lowering the average base temperature by 3.07 K.
The micro/mini-channel heat sink (MCHS), first 
proposed by Tuckerman and Pease in 1981 [1] , offers a compact and 
effective solution for heat dissipation, which is being widely employed 
for heat dissipation of integrated circuit (IC) chips [2,3] .
Commercial 
MCHS usually employs a straight rectangular channel due to their ease 
of fabrication.
It is known that the heat transfer efficiency in the straight channel 
decreases along the flow direction as the thermal boundary layer de -
velops.
Consequently, various non-straight channel 
designs, such as wavy channels, zig-zag channels, and serpentine 
channels, have been proposed to introduce disturbance and promote 
fluid mixing.

Their numerical results indicated that 
decreasing the wavelength or augmenting the amplitude along the flow 
direction enhances coolant mixing and increases the strength of Dean

[12]
employed the Shear-Stress Transport (SST) k - ω model to simulate a si -
nusoidal wavy channel using supercritical liquefied natural gas.
The 
numerical results indicated that the reverse fluid occurs near the inner 
wall in each periodic channel, creating the flow dead zone that reduces 
the heat transfer.
It 
was found that a maximum PEC of 1.135 could be achieved, with the 
wavelength having a greater influence on the overall performance 
compared to the amplitude.
[19] implemented the RSM model 
to determine the best configuration of amplitudes and wavelengths for 
the sinusoidal wavy MCHS.
[20] also employed the RSM model to 
predict the performance of multi-nozzle MCHS with circular fins, where 
the determination coefficients of the Nusselt number ( Nu ) and pressure 
drop are 97.51 % and 98.74 %, respectively.
In their study, as the fin 
diameter increases to its maximum value, Nu is increased by 39 % due to 
the expansion of the heat transfer area and the larger vortices generated 
behind the fins.

Conclusions
This study proposed an optimization for the non-uniform sinusoidal 
wavy mini-channel heat sink (MCHS) using varying wavelength or 
amplitude along the flow direction.
The application of non-uniform wavy MCHS is more effective as 
compared to merely altering the width of straight channels, 
demonstrating the necessity of hindering the development of the 
boundary layer.
Among the design variables (i.e., amplitude A , number of cycles

The MOGA procedure employs a

Based on the principles of evolutionary algorithms, the op -

For Type 3, thermal energy is efficiently dissipated via two syner -
gistic mechanisms. The trapezoidal manifold achieves uniform flow 
distribution across all subchannels, allowing coolant to fully absorb heat 
over the entire heat transfer surface rather than concentrating in partial 
channels. Meanwhile, the wavy bottom wall periodically disrupts the 
thermal boundary layer and generates organized vortices, strengthening 
fluid mixing and convective heat transfer. Wall heat is rapidly trans -
ported into the fluid bulk and discharged downstream, resulting in the 
lowest wall and fluid temperatures. For Type 2, the conventional 
manifold induces obvious flow maldistribution. Coolant accumulates in 
several subchannels while low-velocity regions appear in others. In low- 
flow passages, heat cannot be removed promptly and accumulates at the 
solid – liquid interface, forming local hotspots and elevating wall tem -
perature. Uneven heat absorption among different channels also in -

under high Reynolds number conditions.
Finally, the temperature uniformity coefficient γ at the solid – liquid 
interface under different heat fluxes is calculated, and the results are 
presented in Fig. 16 . The γ values of all three structures decrease grad -
ually with the increase of heat flux. Type 3 exhibits the best temperature 
uniformity, with γ always higher than 0.9 and a relatively gentle 
declining trend. It indicates that the combined configuration of trape -
zoidal manifold and wavy bottom wall can effectively suppress hot-spot 
generation and temperature distribution deterioration under high heat 
flux, showing excellent structural stability. In contrast, Type 1 and Type 
2 show a much larger decreasing slope of γ after 400 W/cm
2
, revealing 
the inherent limitations of single structural design under high heat flux 
conditions.
A clear performance differentiation occurs when the heat flux ex -
ceeds 400 W/cm
2

For the conventional rectangular Type 1, high heat flux leads to rapid 
thickening of the thermal boundary layer, forming a thermal resistance 
layer that hinders heat transport. Meanwhile, the inherent flow mal -
distribution of the rectangular manifold is further aggravated. Insuffi -
cient cooling capacity in low-velocity subchannels easily induces local 
hotspots, resulting in a remarkable drop in γ . Type 2 only adopts a wavy 
bottom wall. Although periodic boundary layer interruption and sec -
ondary vortex disturbance can restrain thermal boundary layer growth 
and improve local heat transfer, it still retains the traditional rectangular 
manifold. The problem of flow maldistribution cannot be eliminated, 
and local hotspots persist in low-velocity channels, leading to a 
continuous decline of γ after 400 W/cm
2
